explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, James says everyone should be "…quick to listen…" (James 1:19). Ears first, mouth second. I wish I'd known that before I talked over a whole set of baking instructions once. The dough and I are still not on speaking terms.
I get why this one tempts you, baker. Lots of us are quick on the draw with our words. But James says everyone should be "…slow to speak…" (James 1:19). The one to be quick at is listening.
Ooh, no, friend, anger is on the SLOW list. James says everyone should be "…slow to anger…" (James 1:19). That's two slow things and one quick thing. The quick one is listening.

I see why you'd say that, friend, but James says the opposite. He says "…man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires." (James 1:20). Anger doesn't get the job done. That's why James wants us slow to it.

That's right, baker. James says "…man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires." (James 1:20). You can stomp around the kitchen all day, and the batch still won't bake itself. Anger just doesn't get us where God wants us.
That's it, baker. James says to "…humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls." (James 1:21). Notice the word is already planted. We just get to receive it with a humble heart.

Good guess, since the Bible does talk about the Lord's discipline (Proverbs 3:11). But that's not what James names here. He says to "…humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls." (James 1:21).

Counsel from elders sounds wise, baker, but it isn't what James names in this line. He says to "…humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls." (James 1:21). The word is what he points to.
Yes, baker. James says, "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only." (James 1:22). A recipe on the counter doesn't feed anybody. Somebody has to get their hands floury.
Teaching is a good thing, friend, but it's not what James says here. He says, "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only." (James 1:22). Doing is what he asks for.
That sounds noble, baker, like a knight in a chef's hat. But James doesn't say it here. He says, "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only." (James 1:22). He wants us to carry it out.
Careful, friend, this one's a trap. James says the man "…goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like." (James 1:24). He doesn't remember a thing. He forgets right away.

Right, baker. In James's picture the man looks himself over, then "…goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like." (James 1:24). James says anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like this man (James 1:23). I think we've all walked away from a mirror and lost track of what we saw.

That's right, baker. James says the one who keeps looking into the perfect law of freedom "…will be blessed in what he does." (James 1:25). He's called an "effective doer," not just a hearer. The blessing comes with the doing.

I see where you got that, baker. Hearing is in the verse, but James sets a "forgetful hearer" next to an "effective doer." He says the one who keeps at it "…will be blessed in what he does." (James 1:25). The blessing lands on the doing.
Knowing sounds right, friend. But James doesn't say it here. He says the person "…will be blessed in what he does." (James 1:25). Knowing a recipe by heart never filled a cookie box.
That's the word, baker. James says if someone doesn't bridle his tongue, "…he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless." (James 1:26). That's a strong word. It tells us our words matter.
Hmm, not quite, friend. James says it the other way around: "…he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless." (James 1:26). A tongue with no bridle isn't something to admire.
I can see why you'd pick it, baker, but James doesn't say complete. He says the man "…deceives his heart and his religion is worthless." (James 1:26). A loose tongue leaves something missing.

Yes, baker. James says pure religion is "to care for orphans and widows in their distress…" (James 1:27). That's religion you can see in action, not just hear about. He also says it means keeping oneself from being polluted by the world.

Good thinking, friend, but James doesn't name prophets and priests here. He says pure religion is "to care for orphans and widows in their distress…" (James 1:27). He points to people in need. That's the list he gives.

I love the royal thinking, baker, but kings aren't on James's list. He says pure religion is "to care for orphans and widows in their distress…" (James 1:27). It's about caring for people in their distress.

That's right, baker. James says pure religion is also "…to keep oneself from being polluted by the world." (James 1:27). It comes in two parts, caring for others and keeping yourself clean. Nice and simple, like a two-ingredient dough.

Not quite, friend. James really does say the second part: "…to keep oneself from being polluted by the world." (James 1:27). Pure religion means caring for orphans and widows in their distress, and it also means staying unpolluted.
